items.title: Bye Bye, Dial
items.summary: Today we're saying goodbye to the Dial and its four modes: low, medium, high, and ultra. A model selector takes its place: You can now pick the model and its effort for each thread. And you can now also switch both in the middle of a thread. The model selector…
items.html:
Today we're saying goodbye to the Dial and its four modes: low, medium, high, and ultra.

A model selector takes its place:

You can now pick the model and its effort for each thread. And you can now also switch both in the middle of a thread.

The model selector now also shows you which of your subscriptions or API keys will be billed for each model, or whether it uses Amp credits.

If you don't want to pick the model yourself, use the Staff Pick, which is the model we would choose.

Yes, We Changed Our Mind

In January we explained why Amp does not have a model selector. In July we then shipped the Dial so you could focus on how hard a task is instead of thinking about model names and version numbers. And it worked: when we changed the default model behind the Dial, nobody complained.

But then we added the ability to Amp to bring your own subscriptions and keys, and Amp became free when you do. That changed what the selected model does. Not only is it what produces the tokens, but it also started to decide who gets billed. medium on the Dial could use your Claude plan, or your ChatGPT plan, or Amp credits, and it became very hard to tell who's paying for which model when.

And that's not to speak of all the settings we had to add to the Dial to make it work in every combination.

So we decided to stop hiding the model and now have a model selector. Now, when you pick it yourself, you know where the tokens come from and who's paying.

And yet, it's still not just a model you pick. An agent is more than a model. You pick the model, and we build the harness around it: each model in the selector gets a system prompt and tools optimized for it, and both switch when you switch models in a thread.

Switch Models in a Thread

With the Dial, a thread kept the mode (and model) it started with. We did that because a model became confused when it continued a conversation that another model had started. But now models are good enough to recover from that.

Now you can change the model mid-thread by opening the selector and making the change. After your next message the new model will be used and the transcript will show a record: "Switched to GPT-6.1 Sol · High".

But some things haven't changed. A model switch still has a price. Prompt caches belong to one model, so the new model reads the whole thread uncached, and the first message after a switch costs more.

Threads that run an agent from a plugin keep that agent.

Staff Pick

New threads start on Staff Pick by default. (Except if you had previously configured the Dial to have a default mode.)

Staff Pick is the model we would pick ourselves, which is Claude Opus 5.5 today. We keep benchmarking models, and we'll change the pick when another model does better.

In Settings → Model Selector, under New Threads Start On, you can also start new threads on the model you picked last, or on one fixed model you choose.

What Happens to Your Dial

Until today everyone used the Dial, so this applies to you.

New threads start on Staff Pick, whichever mode you used last.

Existing threads keep working. A thread you started in high continues on the model it ran.

Dial settings don't carry over. If you changed the model behind a mode in Tune Modes, pick that model in the selector now. If you put your own agents on the Dial in Build Dial, you find them under Other Models.

If you never changed those settings, these are the models your modes ran. The first three are at the top of the selector, and Claude Fable 5.2 is under Other Models:

  • low: GLM-5.3-Flash
  • medium: Claude Opus 5.5

items.title: Boxes
items.summary: Today, we're introducing something new to Amp: boxes. A box is an always-on computer to which you can deploy the many delightful things you've built with Amp. Boxes are small and cheap (the smallest one is $18 per 30 days). But they're full-on computers. You…
items.html:
Today, we're introducing something new to Amp: boxes.

A box is an always-on computer to which you can deploy the many delightful things you've built with Amp.

Boxes are small and cheap (the smallest one is $18 per 30 days). But they're full-on computers. You can run anything you want on them. They come with an agent running on them, too. And agents are great at running on computers.

Today, with hyper-individual software being created nearly as fast as someone can dictate a prompt, a small machine goes a long way and can serve most personal or internal software. Software that you build for yourself and people you work with doesn't need to scale to thousands of users. All it needs to be is available for everyone you want to share with and within reach of an agent.

That's what boxes are: a home for what you build with your agents.

Here's Thorsten showing how he deploys applications to boxes and then modifies their production data using agents:

(Note: prices shown in the video refer to Enterprise plan prices. Personal and Team boxes are cheaper. See Pricing.)

How It Works

You develop your software in orbs. You test and share work in progress in portals. When you're ready, you ask the agent to spawn a box for you.

A box is a single VM to which you can then deploy multiple applications. Each application gets its own URL. The box is permanent and will stick around, it doesn't turn off, and you can deploy to it multiple times from however many orbs you want. (If you want to save money, you can ask the agent to turn the box on and off on a schedule.)

It's worth pointing out that there are no containers or other abstractions involved. A box truly is... just a computer. Because, again, agents are great at using those.

If you want, you can make deployments private or require visitors to Sign In With Amp. Ask the agent to do it for you, it'll know how.

Shared Boxes

You can share boxes with your workspace, so you can run your internal software on a box and everyone on the team can deploy new versions.

Runners on Boxes

Each box comes with its own runner. That means you can leverage how good agents are at using computers by spawning them right there, on the box.

Ask them to clean up the team wiki's database, for example. Or add a new entry based on a screenshot you took. Or ask it to analyze the data everyone added.

Why build elaborate admin interfaces when you can just ask the agent, right there, to modify the state of the running applications?

Pricing

Boxes come in different sizes. They're billed by the minute. By default, they're always on. But you can turn them on and off on a schedule, if you want to save money.

Size Machine Per hour 30 days, always on 30 days, on 6am to 9pm
b1.tiny 0.5 vCPU (bursts to 2), 2 GB $0.025 $18 $11.25
b1.small (default) 1 vCPU (bursts to 2), 4 GB $0.042 $30 $18.75
b1.medium 2 vCPUs, 8 GB $0.069 $50 $31.25
b1.large 4 vCPUs, 16 GB $0.139 $100 $62.50

Getting Started

Ask your agent to create a personal box for you and then ask it to deploy an application to it. Read the docs if you want to find out more.

items.html:
Portals, which you know and love from using them in orbs, now work on your local machines too.

You can ask Amp to start a dev server or build a website on your machine and open it from the thread's Portal tab, regardless of where you are.

Turn on Allow Portals under Settings › Runner in the macOS app, or start your runner with amp --no-tui --remote-control-portals.

Portals on your runner are only accessible to you. To share them with your workspace, start a shared runner with --share, or turn on Share With Workspace in the macOS app, and everyone in the workspace can open its portals.

Read Portals on Your Runner for more details.

items.title: Close the Loop
items.summary: You can now send feedback to Amp directly from your website. Enable the feedback widget in the settings for your project and add one script to your website. Then visit the site with ?amp appended, and the annotation widget is displayed. Click on any part of…
items.html:
You can now send feedback to Amp directly from your website.

Enable the feedback widget in the settings for your project and add one script to your website.

Then visit the site with ?amp appended, and the annotation widget is displayed.

Click on any part of the page and write instructions for Amp.

Once you are done, send the feedback to Amp. The first time, you sign in with Amp. Then Amp starts a new thread in your project and makes the change.

You ship it from the thread like any other change.

Use It

By default the widget is invisible: it only shows up when you open the site with ?amp, or when you have used the widget before.

Click the widget, then click an element on the page and write what you want changed. Click New Comment to comment on another one.

When you're done, click Send. The first time, Amp asks you to connect your account: click Continue with Amp, sign in, and approve the consent screen.

Then click Start in Orb. Amp starts a new thread in your project with your comments, and Open Thread takes you there.

After that, the widget shows up on this site without ?amp, until you hide it.

Read more about the feedback widget in the docs.

items.title: Spaces
items.summary: Today we're launching spaces, a new way to interact with agents and your team in Amp. A space is a conversation with a single agent whose job is to spawn and coordinate agents for you. You no longer have to create and organize threads yourself; the agent in a…
items.html:
Today we're launching spaces, a new way to interact with agents and your team in Amp.

A space is a conversation with a single agent whose job is to spawn and coordinate agents for you. You no longer have to create and organize threads yourself; the agent in a space will do it for you.

It's a new, higher-level way to work with many agents.

After using spaces for the past few weeks, we think this might be the future of interacting with agents. There's something special about this way of working. You operate with a bird's-eye view but can still dive into the weeds when necessary. It's more like sitting in the captain's chair than down in the trenches.

We also found that we naturally moved into the space to communicate with each other. Instead of Slack, we found ourselves taking video calls and discussions into the space.

Here are some examples of how we've been using spaces at Amp.

Collaborate on a New Feature

Spaces were built in a space. Tim, Lewis, Nicolay and the rest of the team shared one called "Spaces v1", dropped feedback, bugs and new ideas into the chat, and the agent delegated them into threads. When they needed to talk, they used comments to chat and then tagged in Amp when they were ready.

Launching and Supporting a Feature

Lewis ran the launch of service accounts from one space. From the space, Lewis could roll out the feature, monitor X, Slack, and bug reports for issues, fix incoming bugs, and send out emails and refunds to affected users. The space monitored user issues and system health for the rest of the week.

Regular Security Reviews

Will gave a space a goal: review recent changes for security issues. Its first run split the codebase into 16 areas, reviewed each in its own thread, checked every finding in another, and kept a summary artifact in the space for Will to review and track.

To start a space, use the + in the Spaces section of the sidebar, set a title and a project, and then tell your agent what to work on.

items.title: GitLab Integration
items.summary: Amp now integrates with GitLab, on gitlab.com and on self-managed instances. Connect your GitLab account and you can start projects from your GitLab repositories. Orbs clone and push as you and come with glab signed in, so the agent can open merge requests,…
items.html:
Amp now integrates with GitLab, on gitlab.com and on self-managed instances.

Connect your GitLab account and you can start projects from your GitLab repositories. Orbs clone and push as you and come with glab signed in, so the agent can open merge requests, comment on them, and read issues and pipelines.

Amp can also subscribe to comments and CI for a merge request it opens. A reviewer's request or a failed pipeline lands in the thread that wrote the code, so Amp already has the context.

A New Orb for Every New Merge Request or Issue

Ask Amp to start a new orb for every new merge request or issue in a project. You don't need to keep the thread where you set it up. See Create an Orb Spawner.

Each new merge request or issue gets its own orb, which reads it and has a summary ready when you open the thread. Later comments go to that same thread. Workspace admins can also run a spawner as a service account.

You manage all of these in Settings → Integrations & MCP → GitLab under Event Subscriptions, where you can pause or delete them, edit a spawner, and see the orbs each spawner started.

Set It Up

Each person connects GitLab in Settings → Integrations & MCP. Then a group Owner installs Push Updates once for the workspace, with one button in Workspace Settings → Integrations & MCP.

Amp also supports self-managed GitLab. See Self-Managed Instances.

Connect GitLab to get started.

items.title: Service Accounts
items.summary: Amp now has Service Accounts. A service account is a workspace-owned account that's not tied to a single user. Service accounts are created by workspace admins. They have their own API keys and third-party credentials. Each thread created under a service…
items.html:
Amp now has Service Accounts. A service account is a workspace-owned account that's not tied to a single user.

Service accounts are created by workspace admins. They have their own API keys and third-party credentials.

Each thread created under a service account can be viewed by other members of the workspace. These threads are multiplayer too, so workspace members can send messages in them.

Since anyone in the workspace can drive a service account's threads, make sure to only assign credentials to it that you would be happy bestowing on all workspace members.

When to Use Service Accounts

Service accounts fit any work that belongs to the team rather than to one person. For example, threads with automations that workspace members want to have access to, even if the person who set them up is on vacation.

We've found two patterns where service accounts work especially well.

Codebase Review and Maintenance

Reviewing every pull request or keeping docs accurate is work that belongs to the team, not to a single user. When a service account owns that work, anyone on the team can step into its threads and steer them.

Here are some example prompts for setting that up via Puck:

  • Trigger a Workspace-Scoped Orb for New GitHub PRs 
    Hey Puck, let's set up a listener so that any new PR that lands triggers a new orb and reviews the changes. **The orbs should be owned by the whole team, not just me.**

    Amp knows how to set up github PR listeners like this. Because the user asked for the threads to be owned by the workspace and not by the user, Amp will use a service account for these threads.

  • A Recurring Review of Public Docs 
    Hey Puck, **start a workspace-owned thread** which scans our public documentation every 24hr and checks it's up to date. If you find an issue, @ mention the person responsible for the change.

    Service accounts are useful for continuous clean up and maintenance tasks like this, which are shared by a team rather than an individual.

Programmatic Work

There's work that starts from a script, like a CI job that spawns a thread via amp -ox every time a build fails. By using a service account's API key for that amp invocation, the thread it starts belongs to the service account instead of whoever set up the pipeline.

Here's an example:

  • A Review Bot Running in CI 
    run_tests

if tests_failed; then
  AMP_API_KEY=<SERVICE_ACCOUNT_API_KEY> \
    amp -ox "Tests failed. Is this a real regression or a flaky test?"
fi

    CI and programmatic invocation of Amp is another useful use case for service-accounts, which should not be tied to any individual user.

items.title: Artifacts
items.summary: Agents in Amp can now collaborate with you in Artifacts. These are documents that belong to a single thread and that the agent, you, and your teammates can all edit. Here are two examples from our real threads. This one is from Nicolay's thread, where he asked…
items.html:
Agents in Amp can now collaborate with you in Artifacts. These are documents that belong to a single thread and that the agent, you, and your teammates can all edit.

Here are two examples from our real threads.

This one is from Nicolay's thread, where he asked whether Amp wastes model calls while it waits on a long shell command. The agent went through 60 of our threads and wrote up what it found: how much the waiting costs, why, and a plan to fix it in two steps. Reading it gets you up to speed on the problem before you decide what to build:

Artifacts also work well for pulling together what several threads found. In Beyang's thread, a user had asked for a rendered preview of Markdown files in the Changes pane. Beyang had the agent build two versions at once, each in its own orb. When both reported back, the agent put them side by side in one artifact, with what each costs and which one to ship first:

You don't have to ask for one. When the agent has something for you to read, like a plan, a report, or notes from a call, it writes an artifact instead of a long reply. The artifact opens next to the thread. Edit it like any document: tick off a checklist, fix a table, rewrite a paragraph. When the agent comes back to it, it reads your edits first and works them in instead of writing over them.

Open Views → Artifacts in any thread, or just ask Amp to write one. More in the docs.

items.title: macOS Satellites
items.summary: Amp now has a Mac: ask it to work on your iOS or Mac app and watch it build, test, and run the app. Port to iPhone Duo New Mac App Feature Penny runs on iPhone 17 Pro. Amp has it open in DeviceHub on a Mac next to the thread. Amp checks Penny on the iPhone Duo…
items.html:
Amp now has a Mac: ask it to work on your iOS or Mac app and watch it build, test, and run the app.

Port to iPhone Duo New Mac App Feature

  1. Penny runs on iPhone 17 Pro. Amp has it open in DeviceHub on a Mac next to the thread.
  2. Amp checks Penny on the iPhone Duo and fixes the layout for both screens.
  3. Then it opens the new build on the Duo, closed.
  4. Amp unfolds the Duo, and Penny switches to the side-by-side layout.
  5. It taps a transaction to open it.
  6. Amp's report: what it checked on the Duo.
  7. Amp recorded the Mac while it checked: closed, unfolded, tapped.

  1. Amp runs the iPod app for the Mac as it is today.
  2. Amp adds a Model setting for the black and red U2 iPod.
  3. Then it drives the app: Settings, Model, U2.
  4. Music, Artists, scroll to The Avalanches.
  5. The Avalanches, “Since I Left You.”
  6. Now playing on the U2 iPod.
  7. Amp's report: what it built and how it checked it.
  8. Amp recorded the Mac while it played the song itself.

How It Works

Your thread still runs on a Linux orb, next to your dev server and toolchain. The Mac is a second machine attached to that orb. Amp can automatically start a Mac, run commands on it, and read and write files, so it decides on its own when the work needs a Mac.

When it does, our server boots a fresh Mac in the cloud with Xcode and the simulators installed, in about 30 seconds. Your orb connects to it and keeps your code in sync, so Amp still edits on the orb and only builds, runs, and tests on the Mac. Screenshots, logs, and builds come back to the thread, and the app on the Mac reaches your backend on the orb through portals.

The thread's Mac tab streams the Mac's screen. Watch Amp's work, or take control of the Mac and try the app yourself.

Every Mac starts fresh, and nothing on it is saved. When Amp is done with a Mac, it keeps it running for 20 more minutes. If you send a follow-up in that time, Amp reuses the same Mac and its build cache instead of starting a new Mac and building from scratch. After that, the Mac is deleted. To delete it right away, archive the thread or ask Amp to stop the Mac.

Morbs Are Dead, Long Live macOS Satellites

Before shipping macOS Satellites, we tried out Morbs: orbs that ran the whole thread on a Mac. But we ran into issues that made the approach unfeasible for a wider rollout. Docker and your backend took minutes to start there,[^1] and keeping a Mac disk around for every thread got expensive.

So we split the thread across two machines. Everything that runs well on Linux stays on the orb and starts fast, and a Mac only shows up for the work that needs macOS.[^2] We're calling them macOS Satellites because they orbit your orb.

Pricing

Size CPUs Memory Price
mac.medium 6 14 GB $2/hour
mac.large 12 28 GB $4/hour

macOS Satellite time comes out of the same orb usage your plan includes, just at a higher rate. Once that runs out, it comes out of your Amp credits, the same way orb time does.

Every Mac starts as a mac.medium. If you need more, ask Amp for a mac.large, or turn off mac.medium under Mac Satellites in Settings → Experimental Features.

Join the Waitlist

macOS Satellites are in beta and opening up as we add Macs. Join the waitlist in Settings → Experimental Features. Each day you click Move Me Up moves you up the line.

Go point Amp at that app you've been meaning to build! Find out more in the docs.

New to Amp? Sign up and get started on your Apple apps.

items.title: Self-Hosted Orbs
items.summary: You can now self-host orbs. You provide the compute and Amp turns it into orbs. If you have compute that can quickly start new machines put them to sleep and resume them equally fast keep them around for a long time scale them to zero, so no one has to worry…
items.html:
You can now self-host orbs. You provide the compute and Amp turns it into orbs.

If you have compute that can

  • quickly start new machines
  • put them to sleep and resume them equally fast
  • keep them around for a long time
  • scale them to zero, so no one has to worry about having a lot of them sleeping

then you are now able to replicate the orb experience within your own infrastructure.

How It Works

You run amp orb provider inside your infrastructure. The orb provider then reaches out to Amp and waits for requests to spawn, pause, or delete orbs. Like this:

How you satisfy those requests is up to you, because amp orb provider will dispatch the requests for orb operations (spawn to create or resume orbs, pause, and delete) to a program that you provide, like so:

$ amp orb provider ./dispatch.sh

In that program, you can do whatever works best for your infrastructure. Here are some illustrative examples:

Docker E2B K8s Apple containers Modal Vercel Daytona exe.dev 
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# dispatch.sh
set -euo pipefail

case "$ORB_OPERATION" in
	spawn)
		docker start "$ORB_ID" 2>/dev/null ||
			docker run --platform linux/amd64 -d --name "$ORB_ID" \
				"$ORB_IMAGE" sleep infinity
		docker exec -d --env ORB_TOKEN "$ORB_ID" amp orb bootstrap
		;;
	pause)
		docker stop "$ORB_ID"
		;;
	delete)
		docker rm -f "$ORB_ID"
		;;
esac

Install the E2B CLI and the e2b package, set E2B_API_KEY, and build a template:

echo 'FROM us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/amp-prod-0/amp-orb/amp-orb:latest' \
    > e2b.Dockerfile
e2b template create amp-orbs --dockerfile e2b.Dockerfile \
    --cpu-count 4 --memory-mb 8192 --ready-cmd true
export E2B_TEMPLATE=amp-orbs

#!/usr/bin/env node
// dispatch.mjs
import { Sandbox } from 'e2b'

const {
	ORB_OPERATION, ORB_ID, ORB_TOKEN, AMP_URL, E2B_TEMPLATE,
} = process.env
const metadata = { orbId: ORB_ID }
const [existing] = await Sandbox.list({
	query: { metadata, state: ['running', 'paused'] },
}).nextItems()

if (ORB_OPERATION === 'spawn') {
	const timeoutMs = 60 * 60 * 1000
	const sandbox = existing
		? await Sandbox.connect(existing.sandboxId, { timeoutMs })
		: await Sandbox.create(E2B_TEMPLATE, {
			metadata, timeoutMs, lifecycle: { onTimeout: 'pause' },
		})
	const envs = { ORB_TOKEN }
	if (AMP_URL) envs.AMP_URL = AMP_URL
	const bootstrap = await sandbox.commands.run('amp orb bootstrap', {
		user: 'user', envs, background: true, timeoutMs: 0,
	})
	await bootstrap.disconnect()
} else if (ORB_OPERATION === 'pause' && existing) {
	await Sandbox.pause(existing.sandboxId)
} else if (ORB_OPERATION === 'delete' && existing) {
	await Sandbox.kill(existing.sandboxId)
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# dispatch.sh
set -euo pipefail
export PATH="/usr/local/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH"

# "$ORB_IMAGE" is the Amp orb image.

ids=$(container list --all --quiet)
exists() { grep -Fxq "$ORB_ID" <<<"$ids"; }

case "$ORB_OPERATION" in
	spawn)
		if exists; then
			container start "$ORB_ID"
		else
			container run --detach --init --rosetta \
				--platform linux/amd64 --cpus 4 --memory 8G \
				--name "$ORB_ID" "$ORB_IMAGE" sleep infinity
		fi
		# A bare --env NAME copies the value from the host.
		container exec --detach --env ORB_TOKEN --env AMP_URL \
			"$ORB_ID" amp orb bootstrap
		;;
	pause)
		if exists; then
			container stop "$ORB_ID"
		fi
		;;
	delete)
		if exists; then
			container delete --force "$ORB_ID"
		fi
		;;
	*)
		exit 1
		;;
esac

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# dispatch.py
import os

import modal

# Needs `pip install modal` plus MODAL_TOKEN_ID and MODAL_TOKEN_SECRET.
APP = "amp-orbs"
app = modal.App.lookup(APP, create_if_missing=True)
snapshots = modal.Dict.from_name("amp-orb-snapshots", create_if_missing=True)
orb_id = os.environ["ORB_ID"]

try:
    sandbox = modal.Sandbox.from_name(APP, orb_id)
except modal.exception.NotFoundError:
    sandbox = None

match os.environ["ORB_OPERATION"]:
    case "spawn":
        if sandbox is None:
            # Modal has no pause, so resume from the last snapshot.
            snapshot = snapshots.get(orb_id)
            if snapshot:
                image = modal.Image.from_id(snapshot)
            else:
                image = modal.Image.from_registry(os.environ["ORB_IMAGE"])
            sandbox = modal.Sandbox.create(
                "sleep", "infinity", app=app, name=orb_id, image=image,
                cpu=4, memory=(16384, 16384), timeout=24 * 60 * 60,
            )
        # Modal execs run as root; point bootstrap at the image user's home.
        bootstrap = "setsid amp orb bootstrap </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &"
        sandbox.exec(
            "bash", "-c", bootstrap,
            env={
                "ORB_TOKEN": os.environ["ORB_TOKEN"],
                "AMP_URL": os.environ.get("AMP_URL"),
                "HOME": "/home/user", "USER": "user",
            },
        ).wait()
    case "pause":
        if sandbox:
            image_id = sandbox.snapshot_filesystem(timeout=120).object_id
            snapshots[orb_id] = image_id
            sandbox.terminate()
    case "delete":
        if sandbox:
            sandbox.terminate()
        snapshots.pop(orb_id, None)

#!/usr/bin/env node
// dispatch.mjs
import { APIError, Sandbox, Snapshot } from '@vercel/sandbox'

const { ORB_OPERATION, ORB_ID, ORB_IMAGE, ORB_TOKEN, AMP_URL } = process.env
const credentials = {
	token: process.env.VERCEL_TOKEN,
	teamId: process.env.VERCEL_TEAM_ID,
	projectId: process.env.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID,
}

if (ORB_OPERATION === 'spawn') {
	const sandbox = await Sandbox.getOrCreate({
		...credentials,
		name: ORB_ID,
		// Copy Amp's image to VCR, then set ORB_IMAGE to its VCR URL.
		image: ORB_IMAGE,
		resources: { vcpus: 4 },
		timeout: 60 * 60 * 1000,
		persistent: true,
		snapshotExpiration: 0,
		keepLastSnapshots: { count: 1, expiration: 0, deleteEvicted: true },
	})
	const setup = await sandbox.runCommand({
		cmd: '/bin/bash',
		args: ['-c', 'hostname localhost && mkdir -p /vercel/sandbox'],
		sudo: true,
	})
	if (setup.exitCode !== 0) throw new Error(await setup.stderr())
	await sandbox.runCommand({
		cmd: '/usr/bin/setpriv',
		args: [
			'--reuid=user', '--regid=user', '--init-groups', '--',
			'/usr/bin/env', `ORB_TOKEN=${ORB_TOKEN}`,
			...(AMP_URL ? [`AMP_URL=${AMP_URL}`] : []),
			'HOME=/home/user', 'USER=user', '/bin/bash', '-lc',
			'exec amp orb bootstrap',
		],
		sudo: true,
		detached: true,
	})
} else if (ORB_OPERATION === 'pause' || ORB_OPERATION === 'delete') {
	try {
		const sandbox = await Sandbox.get({
			...credentials, name: ORB_ID, resume: false,
		})
		if (ORB_OPERATION === 'delete') {
			if (sandbox.status === 'running') await sandbox.stop()
			for await (const saved of await sandbox.listSnapshots()) {
				if (saved.status !== 'created') continue
				const snapshot = await Snapshot.get({
					...credentials, snapshotId: saved.id,
				})
				await snapshot.delete()
			}
			await sandbox.delete()
		} else if (sandbox.status === 'running') await sandbox.stop()
	} catch (error) {
		if (!(error instanceof APIError && error.response.status === 404)) {
			throw error
		}
	}
}

Amp is now an agent in Linear.

Assigning an issue to Amp starts a new Agent Session in Linear and spawns a new orb. You can also mention @Amp to kick off a session. Amp sends its response back to the same session and replies to messages sent along the way. The Agent Session also appears in your Amp sidebar and is fully viewable in Amp.

Assign Amp an issue in Linear.

Follow its progress in the Agent Session.

Then open the same conversation in Amp.

To get started, install the Amp agent in your Linear workspace and connect your Amp account to the Linear MCP in Settings → MCP & Integrations.

Read the docs to learn more.

items.title: See Your Runner's Desktop
items.summary: You can now see and control your macOS or Linux runner's desktop. This is nice for trying native apps that Amp builds for you, such as iOS apps: Turn on Share This Mac's Display under Settings › Runner in the macOS app, or start your runner with amp --no-tui…
items.html:
You can now see and control your macOS or Linux runner's desktop. This is nice for trying native apps that Amp builds for you, such as iOS apps:

Turn on Share This Mac's Display under Settings › Runner in the macOS app, or start your runner with amp --no-tui --desktop.

Your Amp client connects directly to the runner, so it's nearly instant when the runner is on your local network or nearby.

Read See and Control the Runner's Desktop for more details.

items.title: Take Puck with You
items.summary: You can now talk to Puck from ChatGPT, Claude, and other agents via MCP. After developing an idea with ChatGPT's voice mode on a walk, send it directly to Puck for implementation. Puck knows your projects in Amp and routes it to the right orb. In the same…
items.html:
You can now talk to Puck from ChatGPT, Claude, and other agents via MCP.

After developing an idea with ChatGPT's voice mode on a walk, send it directly to Puck for implementation. Puck knows your projects in Amp and routes it to the right orb. In the same conversation, you can check in on your work in Amp directly from ChatGPT.

Puck MCP offers two tools: puck for interacting with your Puck in Amp, and orbs for showing an interactive view of your running orbs with links to their portals.

You're talking to the same Puck you use in Amp. It can look through your threads, find earlier work, and coordinate your agents.

To connect, open Settings > Puck. Click Add to Claude, or copy https://ampcode.com/mcp into ChatGPT or another MCP client, then sign in with your Amp account.

See Use Puck in Other Apps for details.

items.title: First Things First, Faster
items.summary: The Changes pane now automatically puts files in an intelligent order. Amp reads the diff, identifies the files that are essential to the change, and puts them first. If the diff changes, Amp computes an updated order without rearranging the files while you’re…
items.html:
The Changes pane now automatically puts files in an intelligent order. Amp reads the diff, identifies the files that are essential to the change, and puts them first.

If the diff changes, Amp computes an updated order without rearranging the files while you’re reviewing them. Instead, a blue dot will appear over the intelligent ordering button, which you can click to apply the updated order.

The new automatic intelligent ordering is computed much more rapidly. Here is a comparison of the same diff ordered by both the old and new method:

You can optionally go back to alphabetical file ordering by clicking the ordering button.

items.title: You've Got Comments
items.summary: Amp now follows up on GitHub pull requests it opens. Comments, reviews, and CI results show up in the same thread. When Amp opens a PR, the agent can now subscribe to the PR's comments, reviews, and CI for its latest commit. A failing check or a reviewer's…
items.html:
Amp now follows up on GitHub pull requests it opens. Comments, reviews, and CI results show up in the same thread.

When Amp opens a PR, the agent can now subscribe to the PR's comments, reviews, and CI for its latest commit. A failing check or a reviewer's question shows up in the same thread, and Amp already has the context to deal with it.

This is enabled by our new first-class support for GitHub Webhooks. In contrast to our existing, more generic webhook support, the new GitHub Webhook integration centrally handles all requests on the Amp side and then lets you (and your agent) decide whether to forward them to a single orb or to a new one each time. An agent can subscribe to certain events or can set up a subscription that spawns new orbs.

A New Orb for Every New GitHub Issue or PR

Ask Amp to start a new orb for every new issue or PR in a repository. You can also limit it to ones opened with a certain label. You don't need to keep the thread where you set it up.

Each new issue or PR gets its own orb, which reads it and has a summary waiting when you open the thread. Later comments on that issue or PR go to the same thread, so the conversation stays in one place.

You manage these in Settings → Integrations & MCP → GitHub, where you can edit or pause them and see the orbs each one started.

Read the docs to find out how to watch CI when you push to main, follow an existing issue or PR, and ask Puck what Amp is following.

Install the Amp GitHub App on your repository to get started.

items.title: Use Your Claude Plan in Amp
items.summary: You can now use your Claude Subscription in Amp. It's free and available for everyone now. When creating a new thread, just pick Mode > Claude Code. It'll ask to link your Claude sub if you haven't already done that. Under the hood, this mode uses the Claude…
items.html:
You can now use your Claude Subscription in Amp. It's free and available for everyone now.

When creating a new thread, just pick Mode > Claude Code. It'll ask to link your Claude sub if you haven't already done that.

Under the hood, this mode uses the Claude Agent SDK instead of Amp's own agent. But we made it all work: orbs and runners, thread sharing, portals, multiplayer, thread-to-thread messaging and orchestration, etc.

See the Claude sub docs for more information.

items.title: Many, Many Pucks
items.summary: You can now have multiple separate conversations with Puck. We know you love Puck. We also know you've been asking Puck about your recent orbs, a bug fix, and dinner plans, all in the same conversation. Now each of those can be its own conversation, and each…
items.html:
You can now have multiple separate conversations with Puck.

We know you love Puck. We also know you've been asking Puck about your recent orbs, a bug fix, and dinner plans, all in the same conversation. Now each of those can be its own conversation, and each one gets its own Puck.

Press + to start a new conversation. Click the conversation's name at the top to switch between them. Conversations you haven't touched in three days move into Inactive so the list stays short.

Read more about Puck conversations in the docs.

items.title: Plaid Speed
items.summary: Amp now supports Plaid speed for modes that use GPT-6 Astra. Plaid uses OpenAI's ultrafast speed tier, which enables inference requests to run up to 6× faster, with 6× cost per token. Open the mode picker in the new thread dialog, choose a mode that uses GPT-6…
items.html:
Amp now supports Plaid speed for modes that use GPT-6 Astra. Plaid uses OpenAI's ultrafast speed tier, which enables inference requests to run up to 6× faster, with 6× cost per token.

Open the mode picker in the new thread dialog, choose a mode that uses GPT-6 Astra (e.g., the default High mode), and move the speed switch past Fast to Plaid.

Plaid currently works with Amp-provided inference only, as OpenAI does not yet support ultrafast for linked ChatGPT subscriptions. When Plaid is activated, subagents and non-Plaid-enabled model inference will fall back to fast or standard speed. Like fast mode, Plaid can be toggled on or off for an existing thread.

items.title: Opus 5.5
items.summary: Claude Opus 5.5 now powers Amp's medium mode by default, replacing GPT-5.6 Sol. If you use a ChatGPT subscription with the ChatGPT Only preset, medium stays pinned to GPT-5.6 Sol, billed to your subscription. To switch to Opus 5.5, change medium in Tune Modes.…
items.html:
Claude Opus 5.5 now powers Amp's medium mode by default, replacing GPT-5.6 Sol. If you use a ChatGPT subscription with the ChatGPT Only preset, medium stays pinned to GPT-5.6 Sol, billed to your subscription. To switch to Opus 5.5, change medium in Tune Modes.

In our internal evals, Opus 5.5 solved 65% of tasks, up from GPT-5.6 Sol's 61% and Opus 5's 56%. And it did that for 10% less than GPT-5.6 Sol and 25% less than Opus 5.

It's still behind Fable 5.1, which solved 71%, but it costs 40% less.

More Steerable

Opus 5.5 responds much better to messages you send while it works. Add a constraint you forgot, point out a wrong turn, or correct its approach, and it folds that into the work instead of arguing or carrying on with its old plan. It doesn't drop what it was doing, either.

So don't stop it to edit your prompt and start over. Send the correction. Enter steers by default, so your message reaches it right away.

High Effort, Not Max

Opus 5.5 runs at high reasoning effort. Past high, it starts to overthink. At xhigh and max it burns through tokens, scores lower than at high, and costs several times as much. So we stop at high.

Why Not GPT-6 Sol?

OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Sol an hour after Opus 5.5. We ran both.

In our evals, GPT-6 Sol scores about the same as GPT-5.6 Sol, at half the cost. In real work, though, it's much more jagged: strong on one task, off on the next. medium carries most threads, so it needs a model you can count on across all of them.

When To Turn the Dial Up

medium is the right place for most work now. Two kinds of task still belong higher:

  • Lots of unknowns. Use ultra with Fable 5.1 when nobody knows the path yet. Alex had to move more than 5,000 users of an enterprise customer's SSO to new email addresses. He started the thread with:

    We've never migrated… from one set of email addresses to the next before… and we don't really have a way to test it.

    It mapped how sign-in works today, planned the switch, and watched production afterward. The first 41 sign-ins after the switch all worked.

  • Taste and judgment. Use high with GPT-6 Astra or ultra with Fable 5.1 when the hard part is deciding what good looks like. Ask for options, not one answer. Hamish wanted a better transition out of the iOS image viewer:

    Right now it's a hard cut, so can you please give me some options for animations and record them and show me them in line in the transcript here.

    It recorded four options on the simulator. He replied "Ship B to main."

Turn the dial up when a miss costs more than the wait, not because the task is long.

How To Use It

Opus 5.5 is persistent. It keeps going until the job is done, which means it needs to know what done is, and it needs a way to see for itself. These are the habits we use, with prompts from our own threads:

  • Give it the whole app to run. Models are very good at writing tests their own code passes. Running the app end to end is the best way to know it works. Make that one command with .agents/setup, services, and a skill. Tim hit a sidebar bug in our Mac app and asked:

    Repro it in preflight then we can look at fixing it.

    It launched our Mac app, dragged the sidebar closed, and measured the bug before touching any code.

  • Tell it what done looks like, including the evidence it should deliver. Our bug fix prompts include:

    Implement the simplest correct fix, verify it, then explain the bug, the fix, and the evidence that the fix resolves it.

    That evidence is usually a failing test plus before and after videos.

  • Raise the bar when the check is too easy. If it verified against an emulator or a mock, send it to the real thing. When it checked an iPad fix in an emulator, Quinn replied:

    test all of this in the Buildkite iOS preflight and use an iPad simulator

    The simulator caught two bugs the emulator had missed.

  • Hand it the bigger task and go hands off. It holds up well over long threads. Tell it what evidence to deliver, then go do something else. You shouldn't babysit a capable model: if you have the patience to watch it work step by step, you're giving it too short a leash.

items.title: Less Noise
items.summary: Amp now collapses your agent's step-by-step work even more, since you care about what the agent did, not how it got there. (You can still expand the steps when needed.) A year ago, watching your agent's every step sometimes helped, and you probably were only…
items.html:
Amp now collapses your agent's step-by-step work even more, since you care about what the agent did, not how it got there. (You can still expand the steps when needed.)

A year ago, watching your agent's every step sometimes helped, and you probably were only running one agent.

Now? You have lots of agents. You should be giving them harder, deeper work and verification demands. They should run for longer on their own, without you watching them from up close. If you have the patience to watch your agents work, you're giving them too short a leash.

items.title: Shared Runners
items.summary: You can now share a runner with your workspace. Start it with --share and everyone in your workspace can start threads on that machine from ampcode.com. If you have a machine with GPUs, a Mac that's used to build and sign the iOS app, or a dev box in a…
items.html:
You can now share a runner with your workspace. Start it with --share and everyone in your workspace can start threads on that machine from ampcode.com.

If you have a machine with GPUs, a Mac that's used to build and sign the iOS app, or a dev box in a specific network, you can now set it up and the whole team can spawn agents on it:

$ amp --no-tui --runner-id macos-builder --share

Everyone in your workspace now sees it in the picker under Shared Runners.

With --amp-env, a shared runner gets the workspace and project Secrets & Env Vars, but never your personal ones. That applies to your own threads on it too.

We need to offer a word of warning, though: everyone you share with runs code on your machine as you, with your files, your credentials, and your logins. Their threads can also work in the same directories at the same time. So only share a runner with people you'd trust with a shell on that machine. Even better, give the runner a machine of its own. (Better still: use orbs, so that every thread gets its own machine.)

Workspace admins can turn off runner sharing in Member Settings.

Read more about sharing a runner in the runner docs.

items.title: The Mac App Is Your Runner
items.summary: The Amp app for macOS now starts a runner for you. You no longer need amp --no-tui open in a terminal to run threads on your Mac. Open App Settings… (⌘⇧,), go to Runner, and click + to add a folder or one of your projects. Start a thread and your Mac is right…
items.html:
The Amp app for macOS now starts a runner for you. You no longer need amp --no-tui open in a terminal to run threads on your Mac.

Open App Settings… (⌘⇧,), go to Runner, and click + to add a folder or one of your projects. Start a thread and your Mac is right there in the picker, marked This Mac. You can also pick it when you start a thread from ampcode.com, your phone, or Puck.

No More Sleeping on the Job

Keep This Mac Awake stops your Mac from going to sleep while the runner is on and the Mac is plugged in, so you can still start threads on it after you walk away. The screen still turns off and locks. On battery, or when you close the lid, your Mac sleeps as usual.

Read more in the runner docs.

items.title: One Runner, Many Worktrees
items.summary: A runner can now create Git worktrees. Pick a repository the runner serves, hit Tab, name the branch, and the thread starts in a fresh checkout. Your main checkout stays untouched. In the directory picker, every Git checkout on the runner gets a New Worktree…
items.html:
A runner can now create Git worktrees. Pick a repository the runner serves, hit Tab, name the branch, and the thread starts in a fresh checkout. Your main checkout stays untouched.

In the directory picker, every Git checkout on the runner gets a New Worktree option next to it. Choose it and you get a small form:

The name you chose becomes the branch name and the folder name. The runner then creates the worktree as a sibling of the repository: ~/code/amp gets ~/code/amp-fix-flaky-login-test, checked out on a new branch fix-flaky-login-test off the current HEAD. Uncommitted changes stay where they are, in the original checkout. The new directory shows up in the picker right away, marked with a branch icon, and the thread starts in it.

Puck can do this too: ask it to start a thread on your runner in a new worktree and it passes a worktree name to create_thread.

Clean Up When You're Done

A thread that runs in a worktree the runner created gets a new action: Archive and Remove Worktree. It archives the thread, runs git worktree remove, and deletes the branch.

New Folders and Projects Too

The picker can also create things. Type the name of a directory that doesn't exist yet and you get New Directory or New Project. Read more.

Oh, They Understand Secrets Now Too

Runners can also use the Secrets & Env Vars you configure on ampcode.com. Same variables that orbs get. It's off by default; opt in with --amp-env:

$ amp --no-tui --runner-id mac-mini --discover-dirs --amp-env

Every time a thread starts, the runner fetches the variables that apply to it (personal, then project, then workspace) and adds them to the environment of the thread's shell commands, MCP servers, and plugins. Change a variable on ampcode.com and the next thread gets the new value. No restart, no SSH.

Both need a runner on the current Amp version. If yours has been running for a while, it has updated itself already.

Read more about worktrees and Secrets & Env Vars in the runner docs.

items.title: One Runner Is Now Enough
items.summary: A runner can now serve many directories, not just the one it was started in. You can point it at specific projects and directories or let it find your Git repositories. Start a runner and tell it which directories to serve with --dir. Repeat the flag for each…
items.html:
A runner can now serve many directories, not just the one it was started in. You can point it at specific projects and directories or let it find your Git repositories.

Start a runner and tell it which directories to serve with --dir. Repeat the flag for each one:

$ amp --no-tui --runner-id mac-mini --dir ~/code/amp --dir ~/code/sandcastle

Or start it in the directory that holds your checkouts and let it find them:

$ cd ~/code
$ amp --no-tui --runner-id mac-mini --discover-dirs

--discover-dirs serves every Git checkout up to two levels beneath the current directory and picks up new ones as you clone them.

Checkouts somewhere else, or deeper than two levels? Give --discover-dirs a path, repeat it for more, and set --discover-depth to look further down:

$ amp --no-tui --discover-dirs=~/work --discover-dirs=~/code --discover-depth 4

Add or remove directories while the runner is running, without restarting it:

$ amp runner dirs add ~/code/new-repo
$ amp runner dirs list
$ amp runner dirs remove ~/code/dotfiles

The runner remembers the directories you add this way and serves them again the next time you start it from the same directory.

Oh, They Can Update Themselves Too

Runners now update themselves too. If you leave an amp --no-tui runner running, it keeps checking for new releases about once an hour and installs them. Once no thread is running on it, it restarts into the new version, at most once every 12 hours. It keeps its runner ID, its directories, and the rest of its flags.

Turn it off with amp.runner.autoUpdate.enabled: false in your settings.

Read more about serving multiple directories and runner updates in the runner docs.

items.title: Free Agent
items.summary: Amp is now free to use when you bring your own compute and model subscriptions/keys. No monthly plan is required anymore to use your ChatGPT subscription with Amp. No BYOK token fees or limits for anyone (except our Enterprise tier). You pay us for orbs, our…
items.html:
Amp is now free to use when you bring your own compute and model subscriptions/keys.

  • No monthly plan is required anymore to use your ChatGPT subscription with Amp.
  • No BYOK token fees or limits for anyone (except our Enterprise tier).

You pay us for orbs, our remote computers where your agents run independently and in parallel. Or you can use runners on your own computers to run your Amp agents for free.

You can still pay for model inference through Amp if you want, with no markup.

Here's our new free Hobby tier and no-extra-charge Teams tier, which make it easier to get started with Amp and to get your whole team on it:

See Pricing for full details, but let's walk through what changes and what doesn't.

For Amp Megawatt & Gigawatt Members

On average, Megawatt members get a 60% discount and Gigawatt members get a 65% discount on their Amp usage. It's a great deal.

You'll keep getting the same heavily discounted orb usage and model usage each month, plus you can now feed your orbs with tokens from more places.

With this change, you're no longer effectively bound by the limits of your ChatGPT sub. You can tap other model providers or your company's preferred AI gateway/provider (more on that below), all without any Amp token fees or limits.

For Teams

We've eliminated the biggest sources of friction you might hit when spreading Amp, cost-wise and security-wise.

Now, you can invite everyone to your Amp workspace for free and feel the magic of Amp's shared threads, shared portals, and multiplayer.

Everyone can use Amp with ChatGPT subs or your company's preferred AI gateway via BYOK, with no monthly fees.

Power users can upgrade to paid tiers for big orb discounts, while everyone else in the workspace can remain on the free Hobby tier and consume your pooled workspace credits for orbs pay-as-you-go.

Also, you get free SAML/OIDC SSO for the whole workspace if at least one member is on a paid tier.

Finally, we're now formally extending our zero and minimal data retention policy to all Amp users and workspaces, not just to our Enterprise tier. (Everyone was always covered by it for all Amp usage since we started, but until now we could only contractually guarantee that to our Enterprise customers.)

One More Thing: More BYOK Options

Update (September 30, 2026): These are now available to all Amp users on every tier. Set them up in Model Routing. Thank you so much to our Megawatt and Gigawatt members who got early access and gave us valuable feedback!

Today, Amp Megawatt and Gigawatt members are also getting early access to more BYOK providers:

  • OpenRouter
  • Amazon Bedrock
  • Google Cloud Agent Platform (f/k/a Vertex AI)
  • Azure Foundry
  • Vercel AI Gateway
  • Cloudflare AI Gateway
  • Ollama Cloud
  • OpenCode Go
  • Custom endpoint URLs

To try these, configure them in Model Routing in personal settings or workspace settings.

items.title: Restack Your Changes
items.summary: We've added a Restack button that organizes all of your thread's changes into a cleaner set of commits. Use it to split a large diff into logical pieces for review, clean up an agent's intermediate commits before merging, or combine small related commits. The…
items.html:
We've added a Restack button that organizes all of your thread's changes into a cleaner set of commits. Use it to split a large diff into logical pieces for review, clean up an agent's intermediate commits before merging, or combine small related commits. The final file contents stay the same.

Read how to restack and review your changes in the docs.

items.title: Customize Your Dial
items.summary: Update (2026-10-23): Tune Modes now has one role per mode, Main Agent. You can no longer pin a model for the Oracle or for subagents, so the Oracle and Subagents rows in the screenshot below are gone. Task and Read Thread subagents run the same model and…
items.html:
Update (2026-10-23): Tune Modes now has one role per mode, Main Agent. You can no longer pin a model for the Oracle or for subagents, so the Oracle and Subagents rows in the screenshot below are gone. Task and Read Thread subagents run the same model and reasoning effort as the thread that started them. See Tune the Modes for how it works today.

You can now choose the models behind Amp's builtin modes and put your own agents on the Dial. There are two tabs in Settings → Mode Dial.

Tune Your Modes

At launch, Tune Modes had three roles per mode. Today it has only Main Agent; see the update above.

In Tune Modes, choose the model and reasoning effort for a builtin mode's main agent, Oracle, or subagents. Use it to run those models through your own API key or ChatGPT subscription. The mode keeps its prompt and tools.

Connect your key or subscription in Model Routing, then choose models it supports. You can change just the Oracle, or all three roles. Anything left on Auto follows Amp's choices as models improve.

Billing follows your provider connections.

Build Your Own Dial

If you often find yourself using custom agents you built with plugins, like a dedicated code reviewer or a security agent, you can place them on the dial too. Build Dial lets you combine the builtin modes with your agents:

Keep medium and high for building, and add a reviewer with your team's review instructions. A plugin agent can extend a builtin mode, so you only need to describe what it should do differently.

Drag two to four modes onto the dial, put them in order, and hold to save. Use the mode picker in the app or press Ctrl+S in the CLI to switch between them. Workspace admins can set a shared dial too. Your personal choices take precedence.

Make the dial yours. The docs cover both tabs.

items.title: Steer, Don't Queue
items.summary: When you send a message while the agent is working, it's now delivered at the next possible opportunity, instead of being queued until the agent finishes its turn. This means the agent acts on your feedback sooner and doesn't waste time on unnecessary…
items.html:
When you send a message while the agent is working, it's now delivered at the next possible opportunity, instead of being queued until the agent finishes its turn.

This means the agent acts on your feedback sooner and doesn't waste time on unnecessary verification steps.

Most people won't need to change how they use Amp.

If you do find Amp steering too abruptly, we've found that it works well to phrase your prompts like "When done, then ..." instead of "Now, ...".

Ship, Review, and other builtin actions still queue, because usually you want to wait until the agent is done before shipping or getting a review.

If needed, you can still queue from Amp or queue in the Amp CLI.

items.title: Desktop
items.summary: Your orb now has a desktop you can see and control. Use the Desktop tab in any orb thread to get a high-resolution interactive Linux desktop. It's useful for verifying the agent's work when developing for Linux, Android, or the Chrome extension API, or when…
items.html:
Your orb now has a desktop you can see and control.

Use the Desktop tab in any orb thread to get a high-resolution interactive Linux desktop.

It's useful for verifying the agent's work when developing for Linux, Android, or the Chrome extension API, or when working with file formats that need to be opened in desktop applications. It's also useful for computer use, CAD, and anytime you just want a desktop in the cloud.

Modibo Sissoko, an Amp user, sent in a video of how he tests .docx files exported by his application in LibreOffice to make sure they look right:

And if you're curious what Puck does for fun when not helping you, turn on Fun Games in Desktop:

items.title: Fable 5.1
items.summary: Claude Fable 5.1 now powers Amp's ultra mode, replacing Fable 5. It's very good at writing, very good at taking direction mid-task, and very good at working on its own. And it costs less to run. Long Tasks and Proof of Work What won us over is how much better…
items.html:
Claude Fable 5.1 now powers Amp's ultra mode, replacing Fable 5.

It's very good at writing, very good at taking direction mid-task, and very good at working on its own. And it costs less to run.

Long Tasks and Proof of Work

What won us over is how much better it got at long horizon work, at giving proof of its work, and at iterating on that proof. It runs for hours on its own, and when the proof doesn't hold up, it goes back and fixes the work, then proves it again.

Some examples:

  • Hamish told it key presses felt laggy in our iOS app and asked it to find out why. Two hours later it had a side-by-side video of the old and new builds typing the same sentence on an iPhone simulator. Along the way it caught a two-pixel height difference in its own comparison, corrected it, and re-recorded. Typing latency in Safari went from 85 ms to 8 ms.
  • Thorsten recorded his screen creating a new thread on ampcode.com and asked it to make that twice as fast, however long that may take. Fable 5.1 pulled every frame out of the recording to time each step, then found the biggest delay was waiting for the server to finish creating the thread. Creating a thread got 45% faster.
Writing

Writing is where it impressed us the most. So far we haven't been big fans of using AI for prose. Fable 5.1 changed that. The text it produces reads more like it was written by a person. It explains the idea behind a change instead of every technical detail, and draws a diagram when that's clearer than a paragraph. We ended up using it for our new docs pages, where it not only surprised us by writing concise prose but also by running the features on a dev server, executing them end to end, and documenting them with screenshots and demo videos.

Steering

We steer it a lot more now. Fable 5 would sometimes ignore an instruction sent mid-task and carry on with the work it already had. Fable 5.1 does both: it finishes the original task, does what you just asked, and reports on each separately. It addresses every instruction you give it, even several at once. It works great now that Enter steers by default.

Cheaper

And it costs less: ultra threads are about 35% cheaper than before. Cache reads are 75% cheaper than on Fable 5, and in a typical Amp thread, over 90% of tokens are cache reads.

How To Use It

ultra is for the work where the outcome is clear and the path is not. Fable 5.1 is at its best there. A few habits help:

  • Tell it what done looks like, and how to prove it. Example: "The sidebar stutters when scrolling through a few hundred threads. Find out why and fix it. Show me a video of scrolling before and after on the same thread list, and frame times measured in Safari, not Chrome."
  • Steer it while it works. If it's heading somewhere you don't want, say so in the moment. You can also hand it new tasks while it's busy; it addresses all of them without dropping the one it's on.
What the Team Says

Very impressed by Fable 5.1. It's very good at writing, it's very good at... everything really? I'm in a thread where I constantly reply to 2-3 different things and it perfectly keeps them apart. It's like having two conversations at once.

— Thorsten Ball

I've also been impressed with Fable 5.1. Feels less hand-wringy than Fable did.

— Camden Cheek

In my code reviews I agree with its changes more than I agree with the previous Fable's. And I steer it a lot more, because it handles multiple requests at once.

— Hitesh Sagtani

items.title: Intelligently Ordered Diffs
items.summary: The first challenge in code review is figuring out which files to read first. Amp now orders diffs intelligently and highlights which files contain the essential changes. Click the file order button to toggle between alphabetical and intelligent order. Amp…
items.html:
The first challenge in code review is figuring out which files to read first. Amp now orders diffs intelligently and highlights which files contain the essential changes.

Click the file order button to toggle between alphabetical and intelligent order. Amp reads the diff, finds the files that best explain the change, and moves them to the top.

Less relevant files, such as tests, fixtures, and generated code, will be shown in muted colors below the important ones.

If the diff changes while you're reviewing it, a blue dot over the button will indicate that there is an updated ordering. Clicking it will update the diff with the new order.

Every thread in Amp now comes with its own space to talk.

Hit Enter and you're in. Turn on your camera, share your screen, and talk it over with your team while the agent works.

No links to paste, no calendar invite, no other app. The call lives where the work lives.

In the future, we see the space becoming a place to talk freely, alone or with others: brainstorm, whiteboard, talk with Puck or other agents, discuss the thread or spawn new ones... who knows?

We're leaving it open. For now, it's just a space. What you do with it is up to you.

items.html:
Amp can now use a Git identity that is separate from the email on your Amp account. Pick the name and verified email that should appear on commits made in orbs.

You can ask Puck to set it for you:

If you have not added the identity yet, Puck sends a verification link to the email address. Once you click it, Puck gets notified and can make the identity your personal default if you asked it to.

You can also manage identities under Signing Keys. Your personal default applies to personal projects unless you choose another identity in a project's settings. Workspace admins choose one rule for the whole workspace:

  • Amp uses the Amp identity.
  • Amp Account uses each member's Amp account.
  • User Choice lets each member choose.

When Amp starts an orb, it sets GIT_AUTHOR_* and GIT_COMMITTER_* from the selected identity. If commit signing is on, Amp only signs for an email you have verified.

Your Amp login can stay tfc@ampcode.com while your commits use tim@culver.house.

items.summary: Projects in Amp can now include more than one repository. Additional repositories are checked out to an adjacent directory in the orb and the agent is made aware of them. The changes panel will show the diff across all repositories in the project. To add…
items.html:
Projects in Amp can now include more than one repository.

Additional repositories are checked out to an adjacent directory in the orb and the agent is made aware of them. The changes panel will show the diff across all repositories in the project.

To add additional repositories, specify them when creating the project or later in project settings. You can add up to 20 additional repositories per project.

Only the primary repository's .agents/setup script runs automatically on orb setup. If an additional repository requires initialization, you should update the primary's setup script to include this, or ask an Amp agent to make this update for you.

items.title: So Long, TUI Sidebar
items.summary: We are removing the sidebar from the Amp TUI. Why? Because orbs, runners, and cross-agent messages means that there are more threads than ever. We believe the best place to keep track of all those threads is in the Amp native and web apps, with their more…
items.html:
We are removing the sidebar from the Amp TUI.

Why? Because orbs, runners, and cross-agent messages means that there are more threads than ever. We believe the best place to keep track of all those threads is in the Amp native and web apps, with their more powerful sidebars.

The TUI is still great at what it does best: local, interactive threads in a single environment. It already comes with its own very powerful multiplexing functionality, complete with tabs, panes, and more; the humble terminal. Adding our own layer of multi-environment multiplexing on top proved to be a less-than-optimal user experience.

But when you need scale, running multiple orbs in parallel, across your team, the best way to manage this complexity is in the web and native app.

Perhaps some of you are asking "Why do you keep ripping out the stuff I love?".

Because we believe that this is the best way to use Amp, and the best way to develop software with agents, and we think it's our responsibility to push you in that direction.

Using orbs in the web and native app is how to get the most leverage from the most powerful models.

items.title: Setup Without a Commit
items.summary: You can now store scripts to set up orbs outside of your repository. Amp can store pre-clone and pre-setup scripts in your project settings and access them when spawning an orb. The pre-clone setup script gives Amp anything it needs before it clones the…
items.html:
You can now store scripts to set up orbs outside of your repository. Amp can store pre-clone and pre-setup scripts in your project settings and access them when spawning an orb.

The pre-clone setup script gives Amp anything it needs before it clones the repository:

  • Install Git extensions that fetch files during checkout.
  • Configure certificates for an internal Git server.
  • Configure a network proxy needed to reach the Git server.
  • Connect the orb to a private network with Tailscale (known issue: use TAILSCALE_API_KEY, OIDC is not yet working with pre-clone scripts).
  • Install a credential helper required by the Git server.

The pre-setup script lets you work with orbs when you aren't ready to commit setup files to the repository. Amp agents and Puck can access the scripts and set them for you. Give Puck this prompt, or start a thread for the project with this prompt:

Amp will then inspect the repository and decide which work belongs before or after the clone. It will write and test the scripts, then save them in the project settings.

The scripts are also available on the project settings page, where you can review or edit them by hand.

items.title: C++ language server now auto-configures MSBuild builds
items.summary: The Microsoft C++ Language Server for GitHub Copilot CLI now bundles its MSBuild compile commands extractor and invokes it automatically. An agent no longer needs to discover and run a separate configuration skill before it can get precise code intelligence…
items.html:
The Microsoft C++ Language Server for GitHub Copilot CLI now bundles its MSBuild compile commands extractor and invokes it automatically. An agent no longer needs to discover and run a separate configuration skill before it can get precise code intelligence for your project. For more information, including the installation instructions, see the main repository page.

What changed

Previously, setting up go-to-definition, find references, and other language server features for an MSBuild-based C++ project required you to either provide your own compile_commands.json file or Copilot to locate and run a configuration skill before it could generate a compilation database. That extra discovery step added setup time and consumed tokens before Copilot could start working with your code.

Now:

  • The compile commands extractor is bundled directly with the C++ language server, so it’s always available.
  • Copilot invokes the extractor when starting the language server on project open, with no manual or agent-driven setup skill required.
  • Compilation database generation for MSBuild projects is deterministic, reducing setup token usage.

Configure other build systems

For other build systems, you can provide your own compile_commands.json or use a skill to generate one:

  • For CMake projects, use the generate compile commands skill introduced in the earlier C++ language server release by asking Copilot CLI to “load project.”
  • For custom build systems, follow the guide to create a custom build extractor skill.

Get started

Follow the Microsoft C++ Language Server quick start to install the plugin and accept the EULA. If your repository contains an MSBuild-based C++ project, Copilot will automatically generate the compilation database it needs for accurate code intelligence.

An active GitHub Copilot subscription is required.

Help improve the Microsoft C++ Language Server by completing the C++ language server survey. To report a problem or suggest an improvement, open an issue in the Microsoft C++ Language Server repository.

The post C++ language server now auto-configures MSBuild builds appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.html:
[!warning] This is the first full release of mini-swe-agent v2. This includes lots of breaking changes.

This is the largest new release since the launch, focusing on supporting more diverse models and switching to toolcalls by default (as opposed to manual parsing of actions).

What's new?

  • Tool calls: Native tool calling API is now the support, text-based action parsing is still available
  • Multimodal input: Support for images and other content types
  • More flexible model support in general

What do I need to change?

I only use the mini CLI with default configs

No changes needed.

I use custom configs

You might need to move some config keys. See Config changes.

I parse/analyze trajectories

Some metadata fields moved to extra. See Trajectory format.

I use the python bindings or built custom subclasses

You will need to refactor. An agent can refactor your code based on the instructions below.

Full migration guide

Read the full migration guide.

Changes compared to v2.0.0a3:

  • Enable parallel tool calls and use plain text observation template by @aorwall in https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/722
  • Enh: Only ask for task if unset by @klieret in https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/738

See https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/593, https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/594, https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/596

items.html:
This release introduces changes to how we handle Anthropic models, in particular with respect to caching. These are mostly internal changes, it is unlikely that you need to change anything on your end. The advantage is that you can now use Anthropic models also with other "backends" like portkey rather than having to use the litellm class.

Here's the breakdown of the changes:

  1. Simpler cache breakpoint setting: We only apply one cache breakpoint at the end
  2. If no model class is specified Anthropic models are also handled by litellm
  3. All model classes apply the cache breakpoints automatically if the model name suggest an Anthropic model, unless the set_cache_control option is explicitly set to None
  4. Anthropic key rotation is deprecated (as are some minor internal methods)

Changed

  • Change: Anthropic caching applied at end; deprecate cache-related options by @klieret in https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/570
  • Change: Use litellm class for anthropic; cache control support by @klieret in https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent/pull/571

items.title: Aider v0.86.0
items.summary: Added support for all GPT-5 models. Added support for Grok-4 via xai/grok-4 and openrouter/x-ai/grok-4 model names. Added support for gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-lite-preview-06-17 model, by Tamir Zahavi-Brunner. /clear now prints “All chat history cleared.” so…
items.html:
• Added support for all GPT-5 models.

  • Added support for Grok-4 via xai/grok-4 and openrouter/x-ai/grok-4 model names.

  • Added support for gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-lite-preview-06-17 model, by Tamir Zahavi-Brunner.

  • /clear now prints “All chat history cleared.” so you know it worked, by Zexin Yuan.

  • /undo output now shows only the first line of each commit message, making it easier to read.

  • Added support for openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k2 model, by Jack Harrington.

  • Display model announcements with no-arg /model command.

  • Fixed an issue where new settings for an existing model didn't replace the old ones, by Andrew Grigorev.

  • Fixed analytics to support the latest PostHog SDK event-capture API.

  • Bumped dependencies to pick up latest litellm==1.75.0.

  • Aider wrote 88% of the code in this release.

items.html:
New Models

  • Added support for new Gemini models including gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, and gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 with thinking tokens support.
  • Updated model aliases: flash now points to gemini-2.5-flash and gemini now points to gemini-2.5-pro.
  • Support for Responses API models like o1-pro, o3-pro.
  • Added support for OpenAI o3-pro model across multiple providers.
  • Enhanced thinking tokens support: can now be disabled by setting to 0, and improved help text with examples.
  • Increased max tokens for Deepseek models to 65536 for better performance.
  • Updated pricing for o3.

New Features & Enhancements

  • Added --add-gitignore-files flag to enable adding files listed in .gitignore to Aider's editing scope, by omarcinkonis.
  • Co-authored-by attribution is now enabled by default for commit messages.
  • Enhanced commit message generation to use system prompt prefixes, by Luke Reeves.
  • Added --commit-language option to specify the language for commit messages, by Kyosuke Takayama.
  • Skip expensive file tracking operations when --skip-sanity-check-repo is enabled for better performance, by Makar Ivashko.
  • Optimized chat history summarization performance, by jayeshthk.
  • Added custom PostHog analytics configuration options with --analytics-posthog-host and --analytics-posthog-project-api-key flags, by Vasil Markoukin.

Repository Map

  • Added MATLAB language support for repository maps, by Matthew Tofano.
  • Added Clojure language support for repository maps, by Garrett Hopper.
  • Improved kebab-case identifier recognition in repository maps for better code analysis.

Fixes & Small Improvements

  • Improved GitHub Copilot token handling with better validation and error messages, by Vincent Taverna and Sebastian Estrella.

  • Improved inline code rendering in Rich markdown output, by Vamsi Talupula.

  • Fixed Vertex AI model name prefixes in settings, by Wietse Venema.

  • Improved /read-only command to resolve literal paths correctly, by Matteo Landi.

  • Fixed encoding issues in git diff output and LLM history logging.

  • Fixed search block regex to accept optional closing tags when working with HTML content, by Mathis Beer.

  • Auto-create parent directories for chat history files to prevent startup errors, by contributor.

  • Ensure pip is available before package installation.

  • Aider wrote 21% of the code in this release.
