mcpTop.description: # EmblemAI MCP EmblemAI is a hosted Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents a full-featured crypto wallet plus **200+ tools** for trading, DeFi, NFTs, and on-chain analytics across **7 blockchains**: - **Bitcoin** — native BTC, Ordinals inscriptions, Runes, BRC-20, Stamps / SRC-20, Alkanes, rare sats - **Solana** — SOL + SPL tokens, Jupiter-routed swaps, Solana memecoin discovery, RugCheck - **Ethereum** — native ETH, ERC-20, ERC-721 / ERC-1155 NFTs, ETH swaps - **Base** — native ETH on L2, ERC-20, NFTs, Clanker discovery - **BSC** — native BNB, BEP-20, FourMeme bonding-curve discovery and trading - **Polygon** — native MATIC, ERC-20, swaps - **Hedera** — HBAR, HTS tokens, MemeJob discovery and trading Plus prediction markets via **Polymarket**, market research, conditional orders (limit / stop-loss / take-profit) on supported chains, and on-chain analytics. ## Quick start The Smithery deployment connects directly to the hosted EmblemAI MCP at `https://emblemvault.ai/api/mcp`. You only need an API key: 1. Sign in at emblemvault.ai. 2. Open **Settings → Vault Access Key** and copy your key. 3. Paste it as the `apiKey` parameter in the Smithery connection form. Browsing tools (`tools/list`) works anonymously, so you can inspect the catalog before authenticating. ## Auth modes | Mode | When to use | Scope | | --- | --- | --- | | **API key** (`x-api-key`) | Unattended agents, cron jobs, server-to-server, any workflow that mints tokens or sends transactions | Full read + write, no expiry until revoked | | **OAuth 2.0 + PKCE** (RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration) | Interactive sessions where a human can click a browser popup | Read-only `vault:read`, short-lived JWT | | **x402 micropayments** | Pay-per-call across the public catalog without an account | Per-tool-call USDC settlement | The Smithery deployment defaults to the API-key path, configured via the `apiKey` parameter (sent to the upstream as the `x-api-key` header). ## Enabling transactional tools State-changing tools (sends, swaps, mints, conditional-trade creates) are hidden by default. Opt in by setting the `enableTransactions` parameter to `enabled` — Smithery's gateway forwards it as the `x-mcp-transactions: enabled` header. Transactional tools then surface in `tools/list` with a `-transaction` suffix, which makes them easy to allow- or block-list with wildcard rules in the host client. Note: transactional tools also require API-key auth — OAuth bearers do not pass the `vault:write` gate. ## Specialized listings (filter) The full 200-tool surface is wide. For Bitcoin-only, Solana-only, or any other curated slice, use the stdio bridge `@emblemvault/mcp` (npm) and set: ``` EMBLEMAI_TOOLS_FILTER="bitcoin*,*Rune*,*Inscription*" ``` The bridge applies the glob filter to both `tools/list` and `tools/call`, exposing only the matching subset to the host LLM. The hosted Smithery deployment always exposes the full catalog; the filter is a stdio-side feature. ## Categories Trading · DeFi · NFTs · Wallet · Bitcoin Ordinals · Polymarket prediction markets · Cross-chain · Market analytics · Research / web search. ## Links - Hosted MCP: `https://emblemvault.ai/api/mcp` - Stdio bridge: `@emblemvault/mcp` (github) - Repo: EmblemCompany/Agent-skills - Web app: emblemvault.ai - Glama listing: glama.ai/mcp/servers/EmblemCompany/Agent-skills - Docs: emblemvault.ai/docs/mcp ## License MIT (stdio bridge + documentation). Hosted MCP is managed SaaS.

mcpTop.name: Quelvio
mcpTop.description: **Your company's brain for AI agents.** Quelvio continuously understands your organization's knowledge across every connected system — what's authoritative, what's recent, what's persistent, what's temporary, and what should be forgotten. Returns cited answers grounded in your authoritative sources, refusing when the corpus doesn't actually answer the question. ## What makes Quelvio different - **Cross-document supersession** — when sources conflict, surfaces the current truth and explicitly names what it supersedes - **Authority-weighted retrieval** — weights documents by who said them on the relevant topic - **Refuses on weak context** — when the corpus doesn't actually answer, says so. Complete OAuth on first tool call ## Authentication OAuth 2.1 with PKCE. Per-employee identity propagation — each query is scoped to the individual employee's permissions in source systems. ## Pricing Per Knowledge Token model. Paid plans scale with usage and seats.

Query real attestation data — interaction history, success rates, latency, uptime — before your agent executes sensitive operations. **8 tools** for trust evaluation, server discovery, and health monitoring: - `get-trust-score` — instant trust score (0-100) for any MCP server - `query-server` — full behavioral profile with attestation evidence - `list-servers` — browse the entire 14,820+ server directory - `get-leaderboard` — top-ranked servers by trust score - `check-health` — real-time uptime and latency checks - `get-compliance-report` — MiCA Article 12 compliance attestation receipts - `report-outcome` — report tool call outcomes to improve trust data - `get-baselines` — historical behavioral baselines **MCP Gateway Proxy**: Route agent calls through Observatory for automatic trust verification and compliance attestation. Every proxied call gets a trust check + signed attestation receipt. **Use cases**: Agent-to-agent commerce trust verification, MiCA Article 12 compliance (EU enforcement July 1, 2026), pre-flight trust checks before sensitive operations, continuous behavioral monitoring. Published spec: CTEF v0.3.2 (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20285663)

mcpTop.name: ArXiv Scout
mcpTop.description: Search and retrieve academic papers directly from arXiv with advanced query capabilities. Extract full text from PDFs to generate summaries, literature reviews, and side-by-side comparisons. Track citations and references to discover related research and map out academic trends.

mcpTop.name: iAeternum
mcpTop.description: Intelligence Aeternum — AI training dataset marketplace with 100,000+ museum artwork images with 4K token .json metadata. Search, preview, and purchase curated art datasets with provenance tracking. Powered by x402 USDC micropayments.

mcpTop.name: The STALL
mcpTop.description: 293 AI-callable finance and data tools over MCP. No API keys required. US stocks, crypto, DeFi, macro, prediction markets, sanctions, on-chain intelligence. x402 USDC pay-per-call on Base. Built by IntuiTek1.

mcpTop.name: Amalgix Document Intelligence
mcpTop.description: Cross-model evidence pipeline for financial filing and contract intelligence. Two core paid workflows — analyze_public_filing (SEC 10-K/10-Q/20-F, ticker/CIK lookup, metrics, risk changes, contradictions) and review_contract_risks (MSA/NDA/SaaS/procurement, obligations, deadlines, liability, unusual clauses). Plus MCP compatibility utilities: document analysis, web extraction, summarization, and bulk translation. Specialized model routing delivers source-grounded evidence up to 3.8× cheaper than frontier models. Pay per call via x402 USDC on Base or Solana. Document content is not persisted after processing; request metadata and payment events are retained for attribution.

mcpTop.name: AI Answer Copier
mcpTop.description: AI Answer Copier is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that solves the "Final Mile" friction in educational content creation. It enables AI models to move beyond just writing questions to actually generating the files required for teaching and assessment. By functioning as a native MCP server, this tool allows Claude or any MCP-enabled IDE to directly pipe its output into specialized educational formats. No more manually fixing bullet points in Word or wrestling with CSV headers for your LMS. Key Capabilities:Zero-Friction Pipeline: Your AI can now "see" your local export tools. Ask it to: "Generate 10 biology questions and send them directly to my Quizizz CSV." Multi-Format Exporting: Seamlessly convert AI responses into upload-ready files for Kahoot, Quizizz, Canvas (JSON), Moodle (XML), and professionally formatted PDFs. Intelligent Smart-Parse: Automatically identifies question stems, multiple-choice distractors, and correct answer keys from raw AI text. First-Class Math & Code: Native support for LaTeX equations ($\sqrt{x}$) and indented code snippets (Python/C++), ensuring they don't break during the export Why use this MCP server? Generating questions takes seconds, but formatting them takes hours. This server reclaims those 5 hours of your week by removing the technical barrier between AI intelligence and classroom delivery.

mcpTop.name: MAQAMI Travel
mcpTop.description: Search hotels (3M+ hotels) and flights worldwide, read hotel details, then prebook and book. Remote Streamable HTTP, no API key.

mcpTop.name: Guardian
mcpTop.description: Deterministic recipe verification for AI agents. Catches hallucinated temperatures, missing techniques, wrong ingredients, and impossible cooking steps — then suggests one-click fixes. Covers 161+ dishes across 5 cuisines. Also checks EU allergen compliance (all 14 Annex II groups), verifies dietary claims (vegan, halal, kosher, gluten-free), and flags safety issues. Verify against Guardian's built-in master specs or your own house recipe. Same input → same verdict, every time. No API key required.

mcpTop.name: Wellness Pulse
mcpTop.description: Wellness Pulse MCP is a plug-and-play intelligence layer that transforms raw wellbeing data into clear, actionable insights for AI systems. With a single integration, your copilots, agents, and dashboards gain access to trusted public benchmarks (CDC PLACES) and live institutional wellness signals — no analyst required. 🔗 Website: https://wpulse.org 🧠 What It Does 📊 CDC mental health benchmarks by ZIP or county 🏢 Real-time institutional wellness trends & alerts 🗣️ Plain-English explanations alongside structured JSON 🔌 One integration for all AI workflows ⚡ Built For Healthcare teams, universities, HR platforms, and AI agents that need fast, reliable wellbeing intelligence. 🔒 Privacy First No PII. No tracking. Designed for compliance-conscious environments.

mcpTop.name: Synmerco — Confidential Escrow for AI Agent Commerce
mcpTop.description: The only MCP server with Confidential Escrow Mode — HIPAA/GDPR-ready encrypted transactions for regulated AI agents. 46 tools for the full agent commerce lifecycle. **Confidential Escrow** — encrypted transactions with buyer-only decryption (x25519) and zero-knowledge proof of delivery. The escrow system never sees the work product. Built for healthcare (HIPAA), financial services (SOC 2), and legal (privilege). **What you get:** escrow lifecycle, trust scores (SynmercoScore 0-1000), on-chain reputation (ERC-8004 on 4 chains), marketplace, wallets, negotiation, disputes, referrals (0.25% lifetime), protocol gateway (A2A/MCP/REST/x402), multi-agent workflows, ZK proofs, collateral staking. **10 tools work free — no API key needed.** $1K Shield Insurance per escrow. 3.25% flat fee. 179K+ agents in ecosystem.

mcpTop.name: Summiz
mcpTop.description: Find videos and podcasts in the Summiz catalog with concise keyword searches. Skim key insights with Quick Takes, then dive deeper with full summaries and complete transcripts. Create summaries for YouTube videos that aren’t yet covered.

Use the Goal plugin in Cline Desktop to keep Cline working until the task is verified complete.

Customize > Marketplace > Plugins > Install 'Goal' > use /goal

Plugins are TypeScript files that extend Cline's capabilities with:
- Slash commands
- Custom tools
- Lifecycle hooks (beforeTool, afterRun, etc.)
- Dynamic rules

The Goal plugin adds a /goal slash command and an afterRun hook that nudges Cline to verify its work, and only when verified complete can it call the plugin's custom mark_goal_complete tool to finish the task.

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

More details on the patch and mitigations below:

Introducing FrontierCode 2.0: our new coding benchmark that measures a model’s ability to go beyond the spec.

Most coding evals measure a model’s ability to write code that meets a spec. With FrontierCode 1.0, we asked a new question: would you actually merge the PR?

FrontierCode 2.0 is comprised of more diverse tasks, featuring larger scopes and higher mergeability standards. We are now asking: not only would you merge this PR, but should you?

One key feature of FrontierCode 2.0 is underspecified prompts. Rather than including every engineering decision, prompts are deliberately ambiguous, giving the models room to demonstrate their judgment.

The result is a benchmark that is far from saturated, with the top model scoring just 45%.

We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide.
